experiments.title: Volcano
experiments.phenomenon: Soap traps reaction gas as a rising foam

experiments.title: Balloon on a bottle
experiments.phenomenon: Gas expands a flexible boundary

recipe.preparation: Keep dry until the flexible gas collector is fitted.

procedure: Put the vinegar in the flask and fit the flexible gas collector.
Add the baking soda, keep the gas path closed and let the collector expand.
Compare pressure and volume before and after expansion.
observations: Carbon dioxide raises the pressure, then occupies a larger volume when the flexible boundary expands.

experiments.title: Limewater breath test
experiments.phenomenon: Carbon dioxide first clouds limewater, then clears it
experiments.safety_rationale: Limewater is alkaline and the gas path must not allow liquid to reach the mouth.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use eye protection and a teacher-controlled carbon-dioxide source; never blow through liquid or mouth-pipette.

experiments.title: Snuff a candle with carbon dioxide
experiments.phenomenon: A flame stops before every oxygen molecule is gone

recipe.preparation: Use only in the carbon-dioxide comparison vessel.

procedure: Observe the candle in open air, then compare it with the same candle under a one-litre pressure-controlled jar.
Ignite the covered candle and inspect the oxygen remaining when the flame stops.
In a separate jar, add carbon dioxide before attempting ignition.
observations: The covered flame stops near 16% oxygen, leaving most of the starting oxygen in the jar.
Added carbon dioxide prevents ignition without consuming the candle wax.

experiments.title: Elephant toothpaste
experiments.phenomenon: Catalase controls how quickly oxygen fills foam

experiments.title: Magic milk
experiments.phenomenon: Soap spreads colour across a liquid surface

experiments.title: Pepper runs from soap
experiments.phenomenon: Order changes the surface-tension response

experiments.title: Oil, water and colour
experiments.phenomenon: Immiscible liquids layer and the dye chooses water

experiments.title: Lava lamp
experiments.phenomenon: Fizzing layers are modeled; rising bulk blobs are not
experiments.boundary: Bulk fluid motion driven by bubbles is outside this engine's authority.

experiments.title: Density tower
experiments.phenomenon: Density is measurable, but slow-poured miscible layers are not retained
experiments.boundary: The model mixes miscible solutions and has no slow-pour stratification.

experiments.title: Dancing raisins
experiments.phenomenon: Attached bubbles can lift a dense fruit

experiments.title: Red-cabbage rainbow
experiments.phenomenon: One anthocyanin pigment shows five acid-base colours

experiments.title: Invisible ink
experiments.phenomenon: A dried lemon-juice mark on paper turns visibly brown when warmed
experiments.boundary: Only the reviewed lemon-on-paper mark is modeled; this is not a general caramelisation or Maillard mechanism, and ignition remains a separate operation.

experiments.title: Naked egg
experiments.phenomenon: A prepared membrane surrogate exchanges water across an osmotic gradient
experiments.boundary: Shell removal is represented separately by the chalk-and-vinegar route; the membrane object is an egg-white surrogate without yolk, elasticity, ion selectivity or a final-equilibrium prediction.

experiments.title: Rubbery bone
experiments.phenomenon: Acid dissolves carbonate chalk, but cannot compute bone demineralisation or bending
experiments.boundary: Chalk is calcium carbonate with no collagen. Real bone is a collagen–calcium-phosphate composite: acid demineralisation can leave a flexible collagen scaffold, so chalk dissolving cannot predict whether bone bends.

experiments.title: Clean a copper coin
experiments.phenomenon: Acid dissolves oxide and chloride produces green atacamite
experiments.boundary: Solution chemistry is modeled, not a coin surface or shine.

experiments.title: Rusting race
experiments.phenomenon: Iron needs both air and water; salt speeds the same reaction

experiments.title: Hot pack and cold pack
experiments.phenomenon: Different salts warm or cool water on dissolving
experiments.boundary: The vessel is adiabatic; real cup, packet, room heat capacity and dissolution kinetics are outside the result.

experiments.title: Salt crystals
experiments.phenomenon: Evaporation leaves a measured mass of halite
experiments.safety_rationale: Heating brine and an evaporating dish creates burn and splatter hazards.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection; let a teacher control the heat and allow the dish to cool before handling.
experiments.boundary: Crystal amount is modeled, not cubic habit.

experiments.title: Rock candy
experiments.phenomenon: A cooled supersaturated syrup waits for a seed

experiments.title: Slime
experiments.phenomenon: Borate crosslinks poly(vinyl alcohol) with a dose response

experiments.title: Oobleck
experiments.phenomenon: A concentrated suspension responds differently to slow and fast shear

experiments.title: Plastic from milk
experiments.phenomenon: Acid curdles milk and filtration separates the curds

experiments.title: Sherbet
experiments.phenomenon: A dry acid-carbonate mixture fizzes only after water arrives
experiments.boundary: The lesson models chemistry, not taste or ingestion.

experiments.title: Bath bomb
experiments.phenomenon: Water starts a reaction held apart while dry
experiments.boundary: Tablet geometry, fragrance, binders and foam without surfactant are not modeled.

experiments.title: Felt-tip chromatography
experiments.phenomenon: Black ink separates into three coloured spots

recipe.preparation: Place as a compact starting spot above the solvent line.

procedure: Put water and the black-ink sample in the chromatography setup.
Develop the strip and compare how far the separated dyes travel.
observations: The black sample resolves into three coloured spots at different relative heights.

experiments.title: Starch hunt
experiments.phenomenon: Iodine distinguishes flour and dough from a sugar control
experiments.boundary: The colour identifies starch but does not quantify it or model cooking and gelatinisation.

experiments.title: Vitamin-C detective
experiments.phenomenon: Ascorbic acid removes the blue-black iodine-starch colour
experiments.boundary: This is not a calibrated food assay; juice concentration and other reducing compounds remain uncertain.

experiments.title: Yeast balloon
experiments.phenomenon: Fermentation makes ethanol and carbon dioxide

experiments.title: Flame colours
experiments.phenomenon: Metal ions produce distinct flame colours
experiments.boundary: Lithium is not in the current flame series; isolated ion portions are simulation reagents, not physical salt bottles.

experiments.title: Pull iron out of sand
experiments.phenomenon: A magnet separates iron while quartz stays behind

recipe.preparation: Mix the iron and quartz portions before sorting.

procedure: Pass the magnet over the prepared iron-and-sand mixture.
Move the attracted fraction to a receiver and inspect both fractions.
observations: Iron moves with the magnet while quartz sand remains in the source vessel; total mass is conserved.

experiments.title: Which plastics float?
experiments.phenomenon: Bulk density predicts which whole plastics float

experiments.title: Build a water filter
experiments.phenomenon: A quartz-rich sand suspension clouds water; filtration leaves the solid behind and transfers clear water

recipe.preparation: Disperse the reviewed quartz-rich play-sand surrogate in the water.

procedure: Mix the water and sand, then inspect the cloudy suspension.
Filter into a clean receiver and inspect both the retained solid and filtrate.
observations: The filter retains the quartz-rich solid and transfers visibly clearer water to the receiver.
Clear filtrate is not evidence that dissolved pollutants or microbes were removed.
experiments.boundary: The reviewed play-sand surrogate represents suspended quartz and a conserved variable fraction; natural grain sizes, microbes, dissolved pollutants and drinking-water safety are not modeled.

experiments.title: Open-circuit voltage from lemon juice
experiments.phenomenon: Zinc oxidation and hydrogen reduction give a deterministic no-load voltage estimate
experiments.boundary: This is a computed open-circuit teaching estimate with explicit unit zinc-ion activity. It is not a powered lemon battery: fruit geometry, electrode area and spacing, internal resistance, loaded current, power and lifetime are not modeled.

experiments.title: Split conductive water with electricity
experiments.phenomenon: Current makes hydrogen and oxygen in a two-to-one amount ratio
experiments.safety_rationale: Electrolysis combines an electrical supply with separately produced flammable hydrogen and oxygen.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use a teacher-limited low-voltage supply, eye protection and tiny gas quantities; keep flames and sparks away.
experiments.boundary: Pure water remains an insulator; inert electrodes and an imposed current are assumed, without overpotential, efficiency or gas crossover.

experiments.title: Turn an iron nail copper
experiments.phenomenon: Iron displaces copper from copper sulfate

experiments.title: Why salt makes ice colder
experiments.phenomenon: Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point

experiments.title: Baking powder or baking soda?
experiments.phenomenon: Water, warming and acid provide distinguishable carbon-dioxide conditions
experiments.boundary: The surrogate does not reproduce brand-specific staged acids, dough texture or cake rise.

experiments.title: Why soap will not lather in hard water
experiments.phenomenon: Calcium or magnesium binds a declared fatty-soap equivalent into a conserved scum aggregate
experiments.boundary: A declared sodium-stearate equivalent supplies the 2:1 binding rule; foam, micelles, mixed chain lengths, builders and commercial detergent formulations are not modeled.

experiments.title: Grow blue crystals
experiments.phenomenon: Cooling returns deep-blue hydrated copper sulfate

experiments.title: Powder fizzes faster than a lump
experiments.phenomenon: Grinding computes surface area, but not the rate contrast
experiments.safety_rationale: Grinding can throw chalk dust and fragments toward the eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, grind gently under teacher supervision and avoid breathing the dust.
experiments.boundary: The acid-carbonate pathway has no surface-area-dependent rate.

experiments.title: Lemonade that changes colour
experiments.phenomenon: An indicator spectrum changes from blue to orange in the named acidic juice

experiments.title: Settle a sour stomach
experiments.phenomenon: A hydroxide suspension neutralises acid while excess solid remains

experiments.title: An eggshell in cola
experiments.phenomenon: Only the acid represented in cola dissolves carbonate
experiments.boundary: A chalk shell surrogate is modeled, not a whole egg.

experiments.title: Stop an apple going brown
experiments.phenomenon: A fresh cut surface browns with oxygen and time while ascorbate inhibits the visible response
experiments.boundary: This is a bounded visible-response model, not enzyme turnover, texture, flavour, permanent preservation or food-safety advice.

experiments.title: Which metal reacts first?
experiments.phenomenon: Magnesium, zinc and copper separate along the activity series

experiments.title: A fire extinguisher in a jar
experiments.phenomenon: Carbon-dioxide dilution prevents wax from igniting

experiments.title: Colours climbing a chalk stick
experiments.phenomenon: Chromatography separates ink along a porous support

experiments.title: A boat pushed by soap
experiments.phenomenon: The surface-tension event is modeled, but bulk boat motion is declined
experiments.boundary: Motion under a surface-tension gradient is outside this engine's authority.

experiments.title: A pH map of the kitchen
experiments.phenomenon: Some household acids have numeric models and others explain their limit
experiments.boundary: Malate chemistry is not available for a numeric apple-juice pH.

experiments.title: A hand warmer that crystallises
experiments.phenomenon: Supersaturation is computed but the missing solid phase blocks crystallisation
experiments.boundary: No shipped PHREEQC database defines sodium acetate trihydrate.

experiments.title: A borax snowflake
experiments.phenomenon: Heating dissolves borax and cooling returns it as solid
experiments.boundary: Yield is modeled, not crystal shape or pipe-cleaner growth.

experiments.title: Salt or sugar on the ice?
experiments.phenomenon: Salt depresses freezing while sugar produces a smaller contrast

experiments.title: Three gases, three tests
experiments.phenomenon: Pop, splint and limewater tests distinguish gases
experiments.safety_rationale: Flame tests use flammable hydrogen and oxygen-supporting gas; limewater is alkaline.
experiments.safety_guidance: A teacher must prepare tiny gas samples and control the splints; wear eye protection and keep stock gases away from flames.

experiments.title: Nothing is lost if nothing escapes
experiments.phenomenon: A sealed reaction conserves measured mass

experiments.title: Bubble mixture that lasts
experiments.phenomenon: Surfactant catches any generated gas and foam drains over time

experiments.title: A tower of sugar water
experiments.phenomenon: Solution density is computed; slow-pour layering is not
experiments.boundary: Miscible slow-pour stratification is not modeled.

experiments.title: Instant snow from a powder
experiments.phenomenon: A cross-linked superabsorbent network retains water without consuming it

experiments.title: Luminol light in warm and cold water
experiments.phenomenon: Temperature trades present brightness for glow lifetime
experiments.boundary: A bounded luminol/peroxide comparison is computed, including elapsed-time fading and peroxide consumption; it is not the peroxyoxalate mechanism of a commercial glow stick, and luminol-product speciation and absolute photon yield remain unresolved.

experiments.title: One indicator, five jars
experiments.phenomenon: Phenolphthalein follows five points across neutralisation

experiments.title: Hot fraction sets the resting temperature
experiments.phenomenon: A larger share of hot water raises the final equilibrium temperature
procedure: Prepare equal hot and cool water portions, then mix four different hot-to-cool fractions.
Measure each mixture only after the two portions have reached one common temperature.
Order the four readings by the fraction of hot water used.
observations: The final temperature rises in order as the hot-water fraction increases.
Each reading lies between the two starting temperatures in this adiabatic model.
experiments.safety_rationale: Water at 80 °C can scald skin during preparation and pouring.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use eye protection and heat-safe vessels; let a teacher prepare and handle the hot-water portions.
experiments.boundary: The vessels are adiabatic constant-heat-capacity models; real containers lose heat, and pouring or cooling rates are not predicted.

experiments.title: Conductivity follows ion concentration after mixing
experiments.phenomenon: More dissolved sodium chloride produces a larger conductivity reading at the same final volume
procedure: Prepare four equal-volume water mixtures containing zero, one, two and four millimoles of sodium chloride.
Measure conductivity after each mixture is complete.
Compare the readings in order of sodium-chloride amount.
observations: The water blank gives the lowest reading.
Conductivity rises as the amount of dissolved sodium chloride rises at fixed volume.
experiments.boundary: Conductivity is estimated from the computed ions; cell constant, electrode polarisation, calibration drift and temperature compensation are not modeled.

experiments.title: Measure twice, change nothing
experiments.phenomenon: An immediate second instrument reading reproduces the first without changing the vessel
procedure: Prepare five small model systems for conductivity, pH, temperature, pressure and mass.
Take each instrument reading twice without changing its vessel between readings.
Compare the first and second value from every instrument.
observations: Each immediate pair of readings agrees exactly in the deterministic bench.
Reading an instrument does not consume material or change the modeled state.
experiments.safety_rationale: The comparison includes dilute hydrochloric acid and a sealed gas vessel.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use eye protection and teacher-prepared dilute acid; keep physical pressure trials small and use pressure-rated apparatus.
experiments.boundary: The instruments are deterministic and non-invasive; calibration error, drift, random noise, sample consumption and probe disturbance are not modeled.

experiments.title: Pressure rises when headspace shrinks
experiments.phenomenon: The same amount of gas produces a higher pressure in a smaller sealed headspace
procedure: Prepare four sealed model vessels with headspaces of 1000, 750, 500 and 250 mL.
Add the same 0.0037 mol portion of nitrogen to each vessel.
Measure and order the four pressures by headspace volume.
observations: Pressure rises as the fixed gas portion is confined to a smaller headspace.
The amount of gas and starting temperature stay fixed while volume is the changed variable.
experiments.safety_rationale: Compressed gas can rupture unsuitable or damaged vessels.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; any physical comparison requires pressure-rated apparatus, a shield and teacher supervision.
experiments.boundary: The model uses ideal-gas pressure in a rigid headspace; it does not predict vessel deformation, leakage, gauge uncertainty or real rupture strength.

experiments.title: More gas, more pressure
experiments.phenomenon: More gas produces a higher pressure at the same sealed volume and starting temperature
procedure: Prepare four equal 500 mL sealed model vessels.
Add 0.001, 0.002, 0.004 and 0.008 mol of nitrogen to the four vessels.
Measure and order their pressures by nitrogen amount.
observations: Pressure rises in order with the amount of nitrogen.
Headspace volume and starting temperature stay fixed while gas amount is the changed variable.
experiments.safety_rationale: Compressed gas can rupture unsuitable or damaged vessels.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; any physical comparison requires pressure-rated apparatus, a shield and teacher supervision.
experiments.boundary: The model uses ideal-gas pressure in a rigid headspace; it omits leakage, gauge uncertainty and non-ideal high-pressure behaviour.

experiments.title: Copper ions lift Daniell-cell voltage
experiments.phenomenon: Raising copper-ion activity increases the open-circuit voltage while the zinc half-cell stays fixed
procedure: Prepare four identical zinc half-cells and four copper half-cells with increasing copper sulfate amounts.
Connect each matched pair as an open-circuit Daniell cell.
Compare the four voltages while keeping every zinc half-cell fixed.
observations: The open-circuit voltage rises as the copper-ion amount rises at fixed solution volume.
The voltage shift follows activity through the reaction quotient, not the amount of copper metal.
experiments.safety_rationale: Copper and zinc sulfate solutions are laboratory chemicals and must not enter food or drains.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, use teacher-prepared small quantities and collect all metal-containing waste.
experiments.boundary: The voltage is an equilibrium open-circuit value; internal resistance, salt-bridge transport, electrode area, polarisation and delivered current are not modeled.

experiments.title: Electrolysis products follow time
experiments.phenomenon: At fixed current, a longer electrolysis interval produces more modeled electrode product
procedure: Prepare four equal sodium sulfate solutions.
Electrolyse each at 0.2 A for 15, 30, 60 and 120 seconds respectively.
Compare cumulative electrode-product amounts and verify that sodium and sulfur remain spectators.
observations: Modeled electrode-product amount rises with electrolysis time at fixed current.
The sodium and sulfur inventories are conserved while water supplies the electrode gases.
experiments.safety_rationale: Electrolysis uses electricity and can produce a flammable hydrogen and oxygen mixture.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use only low-voltage teacher-supervised apparatus, eye protection and tiny well-ventilated quantities; keep all flames away.
experiments.boundary: The model applies ideal Faraday-law production; current efficiency, overpotential, bubble capture, electrode reactions and gas losses are not predicted.

experiments.title: Conjugate base shifts a buffer's pH
experiments.phenomenon: Adding more acetate to a fixed acetic-acid portion raises the computed buffer pH
procedure: Prepare four equal water portions containing the same amount of acetic acid.
Add increasing sodium acetate amounts of 0.001, 0.002, 0.004 and 0.008 mol.
Measure and order the four pH values.
observations: The pH rises as the conjugate-base-to-acid ratio rises.
The equal-acid and equal-acetate mixture sits near the weak acid's buffer region, not at neutral pH.
experiments.safety_rationale: Acetic-acid solutions can irritate eyes and skin even though the modeled portions are dilute.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and use teacher-prepared solutions; do not taste laboratory materials.
experiments.boundary: The values come from the aqueous equilibrium and activity model; probe calibration, temperature drift and preparation error are not modeled.

experiments.title: A larger distillation cut collects more
experiments.phenomenon: Increasing the requested cut transfers more of the same ternary mixture into the receiver
procedure: Prepare two identical water, ethanol and methanol feeds.
Request a 0.08 cut from the first still and a 0.16 cut from the second.
Compare the total component inventory collected in both receivers.
observations: The larger requested cut gives a larger total receiver inventory.
Each receiver contains a mixture; a larger cut is not a promise of a pure component.
experiments.safety_rationale: Methanol is toxic and both alcohols are flammable; heated distillation apparatus adds burn and fire hazards.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; any physical analogue requires a fume hood, flame-free controlled heating and trained supervision.
experiments.boundary: The generic equilibrium cut omits heat loss, reflux, column efficiency, non-ideal azeotropes and real apparatus performance.

experiments.title: Split heat pulses reach the same temperature
experiments.phenomenon: One 900 J input and two inputs totaling 900 J produce the same modeled water temperature
procedure: Prepare two equal 0.2 L water portions.
Give the first 900 J once and the second 360 J followed by 540 J.
Compare their final thermometer readings.
observations: Both paths finish at the same modeled temperature.
The grouping of heat inputs changes the intermediate path but not their conserved total.
experiments.safety_rationale: Heated water and heating equipment can burn skin.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use eye protection and heat-safe vessels under teacher supervision; avoid touching the heater or hot liquid.
experiments.boundary: The vessels are adiabatic constant-heat-capacity models; heat loss, heater efficiency, container heat capacity and thermometer uncertainty are omitted.

experiments.title: Same salt concentration, same conductivity
experiments.phenomenon: Scaling water and sodium chloride together preserves the computed conductivity while the total portion grows
procedure: Prepare four portions using 250, 500, 750 and 1000 mL of water.
Add 0.001, 0.002, 0.003 and 0.004 mol sodium chloride respectively, keeping salt amount per water volume fixed.
Measure and compare the conductivity of all four portions.
observations: All four modeled conductivity readings agree even though their total water and salt inventories differ.
Conductivity follows the concentration of charge carriers, not the total size of the portion.
experiments.safety_rationale: Laboratory solutions and a powered conductivity probe must be kept away from food and handled with dry electrical connections.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use teacher-prepared dilute saline portions, never taste them, and rinse and dry the probe as instructed.
experiments.boundary: Conductivity is estimated from computed ions; real readings also depend on cell constant, calibration, electrode polarisation, impurities and temperature compensation.

experiments.title: Neutral sugars are conductivity controls
experiments.phenomenon: Changing the amount or identity of a neutral dissolved sugar does not supply ionic charge carriers in the model
procedure: Prepare four 250 mL water portions containing 0.001 or 0.002 mol glucose and 0.001 or 0.002 mol sucrose.
Measure each portion with the same conductivity probe.
Compare the two amounts and the two sugar identities as controls against the ionic-solution experiments.
observations: All four modeled sugar-solution conductivity readings agree within the audited tolerance.
More dissolved material does not necessarily mean more conductivity: these sugars remain neutral molecules in the model.
experiments.safety_rationale: Food-like substances cease to be food once handled with laboratory glassware or probes, and wet electrical connections are unsafe.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, do not taste laboratory mixtures, keep probe connections dry, and rinse the probe between portions.
experiments.boundary: This neutral-solute control does not predict exactly zero conductance in real solutions; impurities, water autoionisation, probe background, calibration and temperature response are omitted.

experiments.title: A filter cannot catch what dissolved
experiments.phenomenon: One silica dose equilibrates into solid and aqueous portions; filtration retains the solid while the dissolved portion follows the water
procedure: Add a small silica dose and sodium chloride to water and let the aqueous equilibrium settle.
Filter the mixture into a clean receiver.
Inspect both vessels and compare the silica inventory in the retained solid and aqueous filtrate.
observations: Most modeled silica remains as a solid in the filter vessel.
A smaller aqueous silica portion passes with the water, while total silicon remains conserved.
experiments.safety_rationale: Fine silica dust can irritate the respiratory tract and laboratory solutions must not be ingested.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use a teacher-prepared wetted silica portion, wear eye protection, avoid raising dust and do not taste the filtrate.
experiments.boundary: The aqueous equilibrium is thermodynamic and the filter is phase-selective; dissolution rate, particle-size distribution, pore size, adsorption and real filter losses are not modeled.

experiments.title: Heat changes a protein
experiments.phenomenon: Egg white and albumin become visibly opaque across their bounded denaturation intervals
procedure: Compare egg white at 20 °C and 70 °C in separate vessels.
Compare albumin at 20 °C and 75 °C in separate vessels.
Inspect every vessel without treating gelatine setting as the same transition.
observations: The heated egg-white and albumin portions become opaque while the room-temperature controls do not.
experiments.safety_rationale: Heating protein samples can cause burns and hot splashes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use small vessels, eye protection and teacher-controlled heating; do not eat laboratory samples.
experiments.boundary: The model records irreversible denaturation and visible aggregation, not texture, cooking safety or gelatine gelation.

experiments.title: Protease cuts gelatine protein
experiments.phenomenon: Only the matching enzyme hydrolyses the bounded protein fraction during the shared one-hour clock
procedure: Prepare equal gelatine samples with protease, without enzyme and with lactase.
Run all three through the same one-hour wait.
Compare the reported hydrolysed protein mass.
observations: Only protease produces the bounded protein-hydrolysis response.
experiments.safety_rationale: Powdered enzymes can irritate eyes, skin and airways.
experiments.safety_guidance: Avoid dust, wear eye protection and gloves, and keep all samples out of the mouth.
experiments.boundary: The model reports hydrolysed protein mass; gel texture and named peptide or amino-acid products are outside it.

experiments.title: Lactase matches milk sugar
experiments.phenomenon: Only lactase cleaves the bounded milk-sugar fraction; no enzyme and lipase remain controls
procedure: Prepare equal milk samples with lactase, without enzyme and with lipase.
Run all three through the same one-hour wait.
Compare the bounded bond-cleavage readouts.
observations: Only the lactase vessel reports cleavage of the milk-sugar fraction.
experiments.safety_rationale: Powdered enzymes can irritate eyes, skin and airways, and laboratory milk is not food.
experiments.safety_guidance: Avoid enzyme dust, wear eye protection and gloves, and do not taste any sample.
experiments.boundary: The model records bounded bond cleavage inside conserved milk solids; it does not claim sweetness or named glucose and galactose inventories.

experiments.title: Lipase acts on oil
experiments.phenomenon: Only lipase hydrolyses the bounded triglyceride fraction; no enzyme and protease remain controls
procedure: Prepare equal oil-and-water samples with lipase, without enzyme and with protease.
Run all three through the same one-hour wait.
Compare the bounded hydrolysis readouts.
observations: Only the lipase vessel reports hydrolysis of the triglyceride fraction.
experiments.safety_rationale: Powdered enzymes can irritate eyes, skin and airways.
experiments.safety_guidance: Avoid dust, wear eye protection and gloves, and keep all samples out of the mouth.
experiments.boundary: The unresolved oil mixture remains conserved; the model does not invent a pH fall or named glycerol and fatty-acid amounts.

experiments.title: Why a boiling pan stops getting hotter
experiments.phenomenon: Past the boil the thermometer stops climbing and the balance starts falling
experiments.safety_rationale: Water at and above its boiling point scalds, and a vessel left on the heat after it boils dry keeps getting hotter.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical heating curve needs heat-safe glassware, eye protection and a teacher at the burner, and the vessel is never taken to dryness.
experiments.boundary: The heat left over at the plateau is spread over the heat capacity the vessel had before it boiled dry, so the temperature of a vessel taken past dryness is under-reported, and the steam leaves the open vessel rather than being followed.

experiments.title: Why lemonade does not change your blood
experiments.phenomenon: The same 0.01 mol of acid moves a buffered solution by 0.08 pH and an unbuffered one by five
experiments.safety_rationale: Hydrochloric acid and concentrated acetic acid burn skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use teacher-prepared dilute solutions, wear eye protection, add acid to water and never the other way round, and do not taste anything.

experiments.title: Weighing the heat of a neutralisation
experiments.phenomenon: The calorimeter counts the warmth twice: once as the lye dissolves and again as the acid meets it
experiments.safety_rationale: Sodium hydroxide is caustic and dissolving it warms the solution; hydrochloric acid burns skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, let a teacher weigh out the hydroxide, and add solids to water slowly so the vessel has time to lose the heat.

experiments.title: Does chalk fizz in vinegar?
experiments.phenomenon: Chalk sits almost untouched in water and gives up its carbon dioxide in vinegar
experiments.boundary: The limiting reagent sets how much gas arrives, but the acid-carbonate pathway has no surface-area term, so powdering the chalk would change the real rate and not the computed one.

experiments.title: Strong and weak electrolytes on one meter
experiments.phenomenon: Equal amounts of salt and vinegar acid read 46 800 and 1 070 microsiemens
experiments.safety_rationale: Concentrated acetic acid burns skin and eyes, and a powered probe must not be handled with wet connections.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use teacher-prepared dilute solutions, keep the probe's connections dry, and rinse and dry it between vessels.
experiments.boundary: Past an ionic strength of 0.1 mol/kgw the reading is a sum of limiting molar conductivities corrected by an empirical factor fitted to sodium and potassium chloride; charge type and ion size are not in that correction, so a 2:2 salt is a weaker claim than a 1:1 one.

experiments.title: Permanganate counts in fives
experiments.phenomenon: Half a millimole of permanganate takes down exactly two and a half millimoles of iron
experiments.safety_rationale: Sulfuric acid is corrosive and permanganate stains skin and clothing and is a strong oxidiser.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, work with teacher-prepared dilute solutions, and keep permanganate well away from anything flammable.
experiments.boundary: The iron solutions end up supersaturated against goethite, hematite and jarosite; those solids are named but not precipitated, because a saturation index alone does not say whether or how quickly a solid forms.

experiments.title: Current times time is the yield
experiments.phenomenon: Four currents on one 75-second clock make four gas inventories in the order of the charge they passed
experiments.safety_rationale: Electrolysis of water makes hydrogen and oxygen together, which is an explosive mixture if it is allowed to collect.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical cell needs a low-voltage supply, an open vented vessel, no flames anywhere near it and teacher supervision.
experiments.boundary: Inert electrodes are assumed with no overpotential, gas crossover, membrane or cell efficiency, so every electron is credited to the product: a real cell yields this much or less, never more.

experiments.title: Five grams of three metals
experiments.phenomenon: The balance says five grams three times; the density meter tells copper, zinc and aluminium apart
experiments.boundary: A piece's volume is computed from the substance's reviewed density rather than measured by displacement, so this is the density of the material and not of the object: a hollow or bubbled piece reads the same here and would float in a real bucket. Asked for a single density of a copper-and-zinc heap, the bench refuses rather than averaging.

experiments.title: Faraday's law, checked on a balance
experiments.phenomenon: One amp for 965 seconds deposits 0.3178 g of copper, a number you can work out before you switch on
experiments.safety_rationale: Copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed and toxic to aquatic life, and a plating bath turns strongly acidic as it runs.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, use a teacher-prepared bath, and collect the spent solution as chemical waste rather than pouring it down a sink.
experiments.boundary: The cell is taken to be fully efficient for copper, with no hydrogen co-evolved at the cathode, which this bench cannot resolve without electrode area and exchange current densities. The predicted mass is an upper bound: a real electrode weighs this much or less, never more.

experiments.title: More catalyst, faster foam
experiments.phenomenon: Four times the iodide makes nearly four times the oxygen in the same ten seconds, and only one vessel overflows
experiments.safety_rationale: The foam erupts out of the vessel carrying peroxide with it, and a potassium iodide demonstration belongs on a supervised bench rather than a kitchen table.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use only household 3% peroxide, fitted goggles, gloves and a tray to catch the overflow, with an adult present; stronger peroxide stays virtual.

experiments.title: The endpoint is not a whole burette step
experiments.phenomenon: A 7 mL trial increment and a 1 mL one both land on 23.000 mL, in four steps and in twenty-four
experiments.safety_rationale: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are both corrosive to skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use teacher-prepared dilute solutions, and fill and read the burette at the bench rather than above eye level.
experiments.boundary: The automatic solver refines its own last increment, so the coarse trial arrives at the same volume with fewer steps. A physical burette and indicator carry an uncertainty of their own that this calculation does not model.

experiments.title: Equal charge, different clocks
experiments.phenomenon: 0.2 A for a minute, 0.1 A for two, and two half-minute runs all hand over the same 12 coulombs
experiments.safety_rationale: Electrolysis of water makes hydrogen and oxygen together, which is an explosive mixture if it is allowed to collect.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical cell needs a low-voltage supply, an open vented vessel, no flames anywhere near it and teacher supervision.
experiments.boundary: The comparison is of cumulative production from ideal electrode stoichiometry; real current efficiency is not modelled, and the gas has already left these open vessels.

experiments.title: The same equilibrium from both ends
experiments.phenomenon: Acid plus alcohol and ester plus water start from opposite corners and stop at the same four amounts
experiments.safety_rationale: Ethanol and ethyl acetate are both flammable and their vapours collect at bench level; concentrated acetic acid burns skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical esterification needs a fume hood, flame-free heating and trained supervision. This is an equilibrium calculation, not a synthesis recipe.
experiments.boundary: An ideal-mixture equilibrium with K about 4, solved from all four amounts including water. It assumes equilibration rather than predicting a rate, and models no catalyst, activity correction, temperature dependence or reaction heat. The liquid ends up two-thirds organic, where the shipped aqueous activity models do not apply, so the ionic speciation is reported uncharacterised.

experiments.title: Filter first, then boil the brine down
experiments.phenomenon: The filter keeps the sand; boiling off half the water leaves the salt twice as concentrated
experiments.safety_rationale: Fine silica dust irritates the airways, and boiling a brine down spits hot droplets of it.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use a teacher-prepared wetted silica portion, wear eye protection, avoid raising dust, and evaporate gently behind a screen rather than at a rolling boil.
experiments.boundary: Doubling both inputs doubles both inventories exactly. The concentrated filtrate is left twice supersaturated in dissolved silica, which stays in solution here until something seeds it; no nucleation clock is modelled.

experiments.title: What burns, what does not
experiments.phenomenon: Magnesium burns to a heavier white solid at 2827 °C; salt in the same flame only turns it yellow
experiments.safety_rationale: Burning magnesium is hot enough to set clothing alight and emits ultraviolet light that damages eyesight; it keeps burning in carbon dioxide and reacts with water, so neither common extinguisher will put it out.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation. A physical version belongs on a supervised school bench behind a screen, with tongs, a heat-proof mat, dry sand to smother it and darkened eye protection — never at home, and never looked at directly.

experiments.title: Hot and cold water meet in the middle
experiments.phenomenon: Equal portions at 20 °C and 80 °C settle at 50 °C, and a spoonful of salt cools it a little further
experiments.safety_rationale: Water at 80 °C scalds skin during preparation and pouring.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use eye protection and heat-safe vessels, and let a teacher prepare and pour the hot portion.
experiments.boundary: The vessels are adiabatic models with a constant heat capacity; real containers lose heat and no pouring or cooling rate is predicted.

experiments.title: Vinegar acid meets baking soda
experiments.phenomenon: The solution swings from alkaline to acid and the carbon dioxide leaves through the open top
experiments.boundary: The beaker ends up heavier than it started because the acid weighs more than the gas that left; the mass lost to the atmosphere is the difference, not the reading.

experiments.title: One pour or two, the salt still arrives
experiments.phenomenon: Splitting a transfer into two stages changes where the solution waits, not what reaches the receiver

experiments.title: Grouping does not change the final temperature
experiments.phenomenon: Six moles of water and a net 200 J reach 25.4424 °C however the mixing is bracketed
experiments.safety_rationale: The branches are heated and cooled at a burner and an ice bath before they are poured together.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use heat-safe vessels and eye protection, and let a teacher handle the burner; the portions here are small but the apparatus is not.

experiments.title: Scale is not soap scum
experiments.phenomenon: The bench computes the calcium chemistry of hard water and cannot make the curd that spoils the lather
experiments.safety_rationale: Calcium chloride warms the water as it dissolves and its dust irritates eyes and airways.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use teacher-prepared solutions, and add the calcium chloride to the water slowly so the vessel has time to lose the heat.
experiments.boundary: Dish soap is a declared surfactant and no fatty-acid soap species exists, so no calcium-soap curd can form: the hard and soft vessels look identical here. The hard-water ions and the carbonate scale in the control vessel are computed; the poor lather is the part that is missing, and naming it is what this lesson is for.

experiments.title: The kettle and the statue
experiments.phenomenon: The calcium that furs a kettle is the same calcium acid eats off a statue
experiments.safety_rationale: Adding hydrochloric acid to a carbonate fizzes hard enough to spatter, and the acid burns skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use a vessel several times larger than the liquid in it, add the acid slowly, and never do this in a closed bottle.

experiments.title: Liquid nitrogen freezes ethanol solid
experiments.phenomenon: One phase change pays for another: the nitrogen boils away and the spirit turns to a white solid at −196 °C
experiments.safety_rationale: Liquid nitrogen at −196 °C causes severe cold burns on contact, its boil-off displaces breathable air in an unventilated room, and a sealed cryogen vessel bursts.
experiments.safety_guidance: Virtual investigation only. A physical version requires trained supervision, a face shield, cryogenic gloves, strong ventilation and a permanently open pressure-relief path — never at home, and never sealed in glass.

experiments.title: Longer waits advance the peroxide
experiments.phenomenon: Identical samples given 30, 60, 120 and 240 seconds have decomposed by 1.2, 2.4, 4.9 and 9.7 micromoles
experiments.safety_rationale: Hydrogen peroxide bleaches skin and clothing and damages eyes, and it releases oxygen into whatever it is stored in.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use only teacher-prepared dilute peroxide with eye protection and clean compatible apparatus, do not swallow it, and never return used peroxide to its stock bottle.
experiments.boundary: This advances the bench's registered peroxide network over modelled time; it is not a new empirical rate law. Real decomposition also depends on concentration, temperature, light, impurities, surfaces and catalysts.

experiments.title: Neutral is a moving target
experiments.phenomenon: Warm water is still just water, and at 50 °C its neutral pH reads 6.63
experiments.safety_rationale: The vessel is taken to 50 °C on a burner and then chilled to near freezing.
experiments.safety_guidance: Use heat-safe vessels and eye protection and let a teacher handle the burner and the ice bath.

experiments.title: The combinations to never make
experiments.phenomenon: Four household pairings the safety layer names precisely, and then shows exactly what they do
experiments.safety_rationale: Every pairing here is a real hazard rather than an illustration: bleach with ammonia makes chloramine gas that puts people in hospital every year, permanganate with a flammable liquid can ignite on contact, acid with an active metal fills the room with hydrogen, and acid with a carbonate spatters.
experiments.safety_guidance: This lesson exists so the four are met in a simulation and never in a kitchen. Do not reproduce any of them physically, at home or at school. If two cleaning products have already been mixed, leave the room, open the windows from outside it and fetch an adult.

experiments.title: The column tells three colourless liquids apart
experiments.phenomenon: Methanol, ethanol and propanone dissolve into one clear liquid and leave the column one at a time
experiments.safety_rationale: Methanol is toxic by swallowing, by skin contact and by breathing it, and all three solvents are flammable.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical separation needs a fume hood, flame-free handling, gloves and trained supervision. Methanol is never a home reagent.

experiments.title: The burette tells you its own strength
experiments.phenomenon: 4.1 mL of permanganate empties a weighed oxalate standard, and the 81st step is the one whose purple stays
experiments.safety_rationale: Oxalic acid is poisonous if swallowed and absorbed through the skin, sulfuric acid is corrosive, and permanganate is a strong oxidiser that stains.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, use teacher-prepared solutions, keep oxalic acid away from food and skin, and collect the spent solution as chemical waste.

experiments.title: The disappearing cross
experiments.phenomenon: Two beakers, one clock, and the warmer one clouds over first
experiments.safety_rationale: Thiosulfate and acid release sulfur dioxide, which irritates the airways and is dangerous to asthmatics.
experiments.safety_guidance: Work in a fume hood or a well-ventilated room with eye protection, use teacher-prepared dilute solutions, and neutralise the mixtures before disposal.
experiments.boundary: Within each integration interval the activity coefficient is held at its starting value while the protons deplete; the acid-base equilibrium is re-solved between intervals rather than continuously coupled to the rate law. The warm beaker is also the first to run out of acid, so after 60 s it is the slower one.

experiments.title: Four small shakes beat one big one
experiments.phenomenon: The same total hexane recovers the iodine to 100.0% in four stages and 99.4% in one
experiments.safety_rationale: Hexane is highly flammable and harmful to breathe, and iodine stains and irritates skin, eyes and airways.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical separating funnel needs a fume hood, flame-free handling, gloves and trained supervision, and the funnel is vented after every shake.
experiments.boundary: Both percentages are computed from phase volumes and the partition coefficient rather than scripted. The reviewed iodine model is restricted to 25 °C; other solutes go through the shared UNIFAC route and unsupported pairs are refused explicitly. The dissolved iodine is not speciated, so it contributes nothing to the pH or the ionic strength reported beside it.

experiments.title: The same fizz with nowhere to go
experiments.phenomenon: Sealed over 200 mL of headspace, the carbon dioxide raises the pressure from 101 to 353 kPa instead of leaving
experiments.safety_rationale: An acid-and-carbonate mixture sealed in a real bottle keeps building pressure until the bottle bursts and throws fragments.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation. Never seal an acid-carbonate mixture in a physical container; a school comparison uses an open vessel, or pressure-rated apparatus behind a shield with teacher supervision.

experiments.title: Identify chloride with silver nitrate
experiments.phenomenon: A clear salt solution goes milky the moment silver nitrate is poured in, and almost no chloride is left dissolved
experiments.safety_rationale: Silver nitrate stains skin black, is corrosive to eyes, and is toxic to aquatic life.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves and let a teacher dispense the silver nitrate; collect the silver residue as chemical waste rather than pouring it away.

experiments.title: The electrochemical series, five ways
experiments.phenomenon: Magnesium plates copper onto itself, silver refuses and says why, and a Daniell cell prices the gap at 1.104 V
experiments.safety_rationale: Magnesium in hydrochloric acid gives off flammable hydrogen and warms the vessel, and copper and silver salts are harmful if swallowed and toxic to aquatic life.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, keep flames away from any vessel making hydrogen, use teacher-prepared solutions, and collect the metal salts as chemical waste.
experiments.boundary: The cell voltage is what the cell offers open-circuit, over activities rather than concentrations; no current is drawn, so this is not what it would deliver under load.

experiments.title: Each pass up the still buys less
experiments.phenomenon: 6 mol percent ethanol becomes 33, then 56, then 81 — and the steps are getting shorter
experiments.safety_rationale: Ethanol vapour is flammable and heated distillation apparatus burns on contact and bursts if it is ever closed off.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical still needs flame-free controlled heating, a vented condenser and trained supervision. Distilling spirits is also illegal without a licence in most countries.
experiments.boundary: The azeotrope is computed from activity coefficients rather than looked up, and the four passes here approach the wall near 89 mol percent without reaching it; the column's stage enrichment is a total-reflux composition cascade, not a literal operating column.

experiments.title: Which cup contains starch?
experiments.phenomenon: Brown iodine solution and cornstarch, side by side with a control that has everything but the starch
experiments.boundary: The blue-black colour is computed — the starch helices contribute a broad absorption band and a `look` at the test vessel reports blue-black against the control's brown — but this script asks `inspect` rather than `look`, so the run it ships with prints the inventory and not the colour. The iodide keeps the iodine in the aqueous inventory without consuming either the starch or the KI.

experiments.title: An ester is made, and the hydroxide never gets to split it back
experiments.phenomenon: The esterification runs; the base that was meant to reverse it is eaten by the free acetic acid first
experiments.safety_rationale: Sodium hydroxide is caustic, ethanol and ethyl acetate are flammable, and the neutralisation warms the vessel by nine degrees on its own.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical esterification needs a fume hood, flame-free heating, gloves and trained supervision.
experiments.boundary: Both transformations are curated and each runs only when asked: a beaker of vinegar and spirit does not esterify by itself. In this dilute vessel the esterification reaches only about 3 mmol, and the 0.1 mol of hydroxide is spent neutralising the remaining acetic acid, so the requested saponification finds no limiting reactant left and reports no conversion. The ester made in the first half stays in the beaker.

experiments.title: One cut from a three-component mixture
experiments.phenomenon: Water, methanol and isopropanol split between flask and receiver with every component still accounted for
experiments.safety_rationale: Methanol is toxic by swallowing, by skin contact and by breathing it, and both alcohols are flammable.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation; a physical cut needs a fume hood, flame-free controlled heating and trained supervision. Methanol is never a home reagent.
experiments.boundary: An ideal-liquid Raoult and Rayleigh approximation with constant-latent-heat vapour pressures, bounded within 40 K of every normal boiling point. Activity coefficients, azeotropes and boiling shifts from dissolved solutes are not predicted, and the reported energy counts only the withdrawn condensate's latent heat.

experiments.title: Phosphoric acid meets the burette
experiments.phenomenon: One acid gives up three protons, and the pH climbs 1.64, 2.20, 4.40, 6.63, 9.20 in steps rather than a line
experiments.safety_rationale: Phosphoric acid and sodium hydroxide are both corrosive to skin and eyes, and each addition warms the vessel.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, use teacher-prepared dilute solutions, and add the base in small portions with stirring.

experiments.title: Titration, one addition at a time
experiments.phenomenon: The pH crawls from 1.75 to 2.75 over nine millimoles of base and then jumps to 11.52 over the last three
experiments.safety_rationale: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are both corrosive to skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use teacher-prepared dilute solutions, and fill and read the burette at the bench rather than above eye level.

experiments.title: Follow the precipitate and the filtrate to dryness
experiments.phenomenon: The barium sulfate stays in the filter; its spectator ions follow the water and are still there when the water is gone
experiments.safety_rationale: Soluble barium salts are acutely toxic if swallowed, and barium chloride is the salt this lesson starts from.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation. A physical version requires trained supervision, eye protection, gloves and hazardous-waste collection — barium solutions never go into a domestic sink.
experiments.boundary: The precipitation and the filtration are both computed and the element totals balance across each source-and-receiver pair. Drying the second filtrate is where the model stops: with the last of the water gone, the barium, chloride, sodium and sulfate ions are still reported as dissolved, which is not a state a beaker can be in. What they crystallise into is not decidable from the ions alone, and the bench refuses to guess rather than inventing a solid.

experiments.title: A salt pulse through a water column
experiments.phenomenon: Pushed through three cells, the salt front spreads out exactly as the binomial coefficients say
experiments.boundary: The column is three ideal well-mixed cells advanced at a fixed Courant number; there is no packing, no dispersion coefficient and no real flow field.

experiments.title: Two limits on one carbon-dioxide ledger
experiments.phenomenon: More acid buys more gas, until the bicarbonate runs out and stops selling
experiments.safety_rationale: Acid and carbonate fizz hard enough to foam out of a vessel that is too small, and the acid burns skin and eyes.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection, use small teacher-prepared portions in a vessel several times larger than the liquid, and never seal an acid-and-carbonate mixture.
experiments.boundary: These are equilibrium inventory calculations rather than a fizz-rate or bubble-volume prediction; foam height, nucleation, gas capture, heat exchange and mixing time are all absent.

experiments.title: Two roads, one temperature
experiments.phenomenon: Acid into base or base into acid, the thermometer ends on 48.76 °C either way
experiments.safety_rationale: Sodium hydroxide is caustic, hydrochloric acid is corrosive, and the neutralisation itself takes the vessel up by twenty-four degrees.
experiments.safety_guidance: Wear eye protection and gloves, use heat-safe vessels and teacher-prepared dilute solutions, and add one reagent to the other slowly.

experiments.title: Warm the gas, stop before the burst
experiments.phenomenon: 0, 100 and 200 J read 122, 201 and 276 kPa; 400 J takes the vessel past 405 and it goes
experiments.safety_rationale: A sealed vessel heated past its rating bursts and throws glass, and this is the one experiment here that is designed to reach that point.
experiments.safety_guidance: Treat this as a simulation. The burst is evidence, not an invitation to retry it; a physical comparison needs pressure-rated apparatus, a shield and teacher supervision, and stops at the third vessel.
experiments.boundary: The pressure is ideal-gas in a rigid headspace against a single glass rating; vessel deformation, fatigue, gauge uncertainty and the real spread of rupture strengths are not modelled.

experiments.title: Why an apple floats and a potato sinks
experiments.phenomenon: Buoyancy belongs to the whole object, pores and trapped air included — which is how a stone made of silica floats
experiments.boundary: The three objects carry reviewed whole-object densities, so changing an ingredient's density would be the wrong calculation. Water entering the pumice's pores is not simulated, so it never waterlogs and sinks.
